item.title: Shoulder Literature — 2026-11-14
item.itunes:author: Eric R. Wagner, MD, MSc
item.description: Weekly Shoulder Surgery Literature Digest — 2026-11-14 Pulled from PubMed across JSES, JSES International, AJSM, JAAOS, Arthroscopy, JBJS Am, and Bone & Joint Journal. This is a print-issue catch-up edition. The standard 7-day window (2026-11-07 to 2026-11-14) was swept and then widened to 14 days per protocol, and both windows returned zero new ahead-of-print shoulder articles: the mid-week digest dated 2026-11-12 had already covered everything the seven journals posted through Thursday, and the only shoulder items entered since then are a letter to Arthroscopy on Sugaya III re-tears and the CUIstow letter-and-reply pair, all excluded by rule. Rather than ship an empty week, this digest covers 20 shoulder clinical and translational papers that have never appeared in a Tutor digest because their ahead-of-print entry dates (March to June 2026) predate Tutor's first run on 2026-07-03, and that have now reached print in the September, October, and November 2026 issues — Arthroscopy (12), JBJS Am (4), AJSM (3), and JAAOS (1). For most readers these are new; they are the papers now sitting in the physical journals on the desk. The week's center of gravity is the large and irreparable rotator cuff tear, with seven papers on augmentation, superior capsular reconstruction, and tendon transfer. Two Korean cohorts make the case for dermal allograft: from Samsung Medical Center, 738 arthroscopic repairs stratified by the Rotator Cuff Healing Index show that patch augmentation cut the retear rate from 36.6% to 21.6% once the index reached 7 or higher, and from Nowon Eulji Medical Center, 36 propensity-matched pairs of large-to-massive tears with only partial repair possible show a retear rate of 8.3% with a human dermal allograft patch versus 33.3% without, with better ASES, Constant, and SANE scores. A McMaster decision-tree analysis then prices it: allograft augmentation costs about $1,900 more than conventional repair and comes in at $18,844 per QALY, with xenograft dominated at $62,620 per QALY, both cost-effective as long as the augmented retear rate stays below 27%. On superior capsular reconstruction, a DOCS Health / Kaiser Southern California series finds that a 6 mm dermal allograft had a 27% graft tear rate and no lateral-sided failures versus 64% and 40% with a 3 mm graft, with a 17-point ASES difference, and an Ewha Womans University cadaveric study shows a 4.8 mm porcine xenograft restores superior translation and subacromial pressure closer to intact than a 2.1 mm single-layer human allograft. On transfers, the Yeosu Baek Hospital group reports two series: arthroscopically assisted latissimus dorsi transfer in 33 shoulders at a minimum ten years, with Constant improving from 48 to 63, 58% of transfers intact on MRI, Hamada progression in 36% that did not cost function, and only 9% converted to reverse arthroplasty; and lower trapezius transfer in 75 shoulders, where a reparable subscapularis tear did not change ASES or Constant but did blunt ga

item.title: Shoulder Literature — 2026-11-12
item.itunes:author: Eric R. Wagner, MD, MSc
item.description: Weekly Shoulder Surgery Literature Digest — 2026-11-12 Pulled from PubMed across JSES, JSES International, AJSM, JAAOS, Arthroscopy, JBJS Am, and Bone & Joint Journal. This digest covers 2026-11-05 to 2026-11-12, a standard 7-day window run mid-week (the previous digest, dated 2026-11-07, had already swept entries through 2026-11-08, so everything here is new since then). 11 shoulder-specific clinical and translational articles qualified — JSES (9) and JSES International (2). It is an arthroplasty- and cuff-heavy week: three registry or multicenter arthroplasty cohorts, an implant biomechanics study, a posture-to-scapula computational model, two prospective multicenter cuff cohorts, a robotic tendon-transfer biomechanics study, an arthroscopic nerve-release series, a second-look arthroscopy study of manipulation for frozen shoulder, and a community screening study of asymptomatic cuff tears. Arthroplasty leads. From the Dutch Arthroplasty Register, 1,683 anatomic total shoulders with Walch A glenoids and fully cemented all-polyethylene components show that glenohumeral radial mismatch below versus at or above 5 mm does not change revision for aseptic glenoid loosening (98.5% versus 98.2% six-year survival), though high mismatch carried a higher hazard of revision for instability on a small number of events. From the Kaiser Permanente Shoulder Arthroplasty Registry, 1,415 reverse arthroplasties for proximal humerus fracture show no difference in five-year all-cause revision between uncemented and cemented humeral stems after propensity weighting (HR 1.20), nor in revision for dislocation or infection. A multicenter cohort of 817 anatomic arthroplasties led from the University of Virginia finds that stemless implants are associated with less opioid use at the 10–14 day visit (35% versus 49%, relative risk 0.72) even though pain scores themselves do not differ. From Rothman, bench testing of the DePuy INHANCE modular convertible glenoid shows less tensile displacement after cyclic rocking than an all-polyethylene glenoid and substantially greater resistance to liner dissociation than a competing platform system. And an Arthrex Munich computational study shows that simple lateral photographs of upper-body posture predict upright three-dimensional scapular orientation (thoracic kyphosis index R² ≥ 0.94), offering a practical adjunct to supine-CT planning. The rotator cuff theme is anchored by two Swiss multicenter cohorts. From the ARCRPred cohort (19 centers), 445 patients who had biceps tenodesis during arthroscopic cuff repair show a Popeye sign three times more often after suprapectoral than subpectoral tenodesis (15% versus 5%), with no difference in groove pain, function, or complications, and a small strength difference that did not reach clinical importance. item.title: Shoulder Literature — 2026-11-07
item.itunes:author: Eric R. Wagner, MD, MSc
item.description: Weekly Shoulder Surgery Literature Digest — 2026-11-07 Pulled from PubMed across JSES, JSES International, AJSM, JAAOS, Arthroscopy, JBJS Am, and Bone & Joint Journal. This digest covers 2026-11-01 to 2026-11-07, the standard 7-day window, picking up where the 2026-11-01 catch-up digest ended. 11 shoulder-specific clinical and translational articles qualified — JSES (7), JAAOS (2), JBJS Am (1), and AJSM (1). A quieter week than usual, but a substantive one: two consensus documents, three systematic reviews or meta-analyses, a cost-effectiveness model, a clinical cohort, a cadaveric biomechanics study, a current-concepts review, and two mechanistic animal studies. Arthroplasty and infection lead. Surena Namdari and the Shoulder Group of the 2025 International Consensus Meeting on Orthopedic Infections publish two proceedings papers in JSES. The diagnosis document reaches consensus on 31 of 32 questions: humeral component loosening, ESR, and CRP are endorsed as diagnostic criteria; cloudy fluid, postoperative stiffness, serum WBC, and D-dimer are not; arthroscopic tissue biopsy, frozen section, and ultrasound-guided aspiration or synovial biopsy are supported as adjuncts, along with five intraoperative specimens and prolonged aerobic and anaerobic culture; next-generation sequencing and synovial neutrophil testing are supported as adjuncts while alpha-defensin is judged insufficiently validated; and routine bone scan, MRI, CT, SPECT, or PET/CT is not supported. The prevention document reaches consensus on all 25 questions: male sex and malnutrition are risk factors, moderate-strength evidence supports no corticosteroid injection within 3 months of arthroplasty, alcohol-based skin prep and avoidance of razor shaving are endorsed, and the evidence for intrawound antibiotics, antiseptic irrigation, iodine drapes, tranexamic acid, and arthroplasty type was judged insufficient. From Beijing Jishuitan Hospital, a meta-analysis of 65 studies is the first to pool pre- to postoperative change in ASES and Constant scores after reverse arthroplasty: prior shoulder surgery is the only consistent patient-level predictor of smaller gains, age and obesity do not matter, lower socioeconomic status predicts worse ASES, and cemented humeral fixation and subscapularis repair are associated with greater improvement. Montefiore finds that CT-measured local adipose-to-deltoid and soft-tissue-to-bone ratios do not predict surgical time, in-hospital complications, or 90-day ED return after 200 primary reverses, while a preoperative ED visit (OR 6.8) and anxiety (OR 2.5–2.6) do. And a JAAOS current-concepts review from Colorado lays out the options for glenohumeral arthritis in the young patient, from comprehensive arthroscopic management through pyrocarbon hemiarthroplasty, ream-and-run, stemless anatomic replacement with inlay or inset glenoids, and the expanding role of reverse arthroplasty. item.title: Shoulder Literature — 2026-11-01
item.itunes:author: Eric R. Wagner, MD, MSc
item.description: Weekly Shoulder Surgery Literature Digest — 2026-11-01 Pulled from PubMed across JSES, JSES International, AJSM, JAAOS, Arthroscopy, JBJS Am, and Bone & Joint Journal. This digest covers 2026-10-18 to 2026-11-01, a 14-day window. The scheduler did not fire on either 2026-10-24 or 2026-10-31, so the week of 10-18 to 10-24 had never been swept; rather than leave a hole in the archive, this run widened to 14 days and covers both weeks together. 22 shoulder-specific clinical and translational articles qualified — JSES (7), Arthroscopy (7), JSES International (6), and AJSM (2). Arthroplasty leads. The New Zealand Joint Registry reports 8,601 reverse arthroplasties and finds that the inverted-bearing design with a polyethylene glenosphere carried a 43% lower adjusted revision rate than a conventional metal glenosphere, with fewer revisions for infection and dislocation and identical Oxford scores out to 10 years. Johns Hopkins shows in a systematic review that "survival" after reverse arthroplasty means different things in different papers: with one standardized definition, 10-year survival of the whole construct is 82.7% and of the metal components 89.5%, well below the 94–95% that registries report. Two risk tools arrive: the SHORD score (Baylor and Fondren), a 16-item preoperative predictor of non-home discharge built on 29,382 NSQIP arthroplasties with an AUROC of 0.82, and a PearlDiver study from Arizona showing that a myocardial infarction within 6 months of total shoulder arthroplasty carries roughly 10-fold odds of a postoperative MI. A Belgian cohort of 698 reverses finds that a 2-week sling, rather than 6 weeks, does not increase acromial or scapular spine stress fractures, and a French bench study shows that humeral component migration after stemless arthroplasty is detected on a true neutral-rotation AP view 91% of the time but only 29% of the time on an internal-rotation view. Werthel and Gerber report that scapular morphology is largely symmetrical bilaterally in 304 healthy CT pairs, so an at-risk posterior acromion is a constitutional phenotype rather than a one-sided variant. Instability is the second theme. The Steadman Clinic follows 96 patients aged 24 or younger with less than 10% glenoid bone loss for a mean of 5.7 years after isolated arthroscopic Bankart repair and reports a 33% recurrence rate and 20% revision rate, with contact sport the one predictor of failure. A TriNetX comparison from Virginia Commonwealth finds that patients stabilized after recurrent rather than first-time dislocation have more than 10 times the short-term redislocation rate. UCSF uses PearlDiver to show Latarjet has a lower 2-year reoperation rate than the anterior free bone block (8.7% vs 13.4%) with the same nerve-injury rate, and Duke offers the first clinical look at the global track angle, finding a cutoff near 66° for off-track lesions and a glenoid angle of about 23° corresponding to 13.5% bone loss. item.title: Shoulder Literature — 2026-10-17
item.itunes:author: Eric R. Wagner, MD, MSc
item.description: Weekly Shoulder Surgery Literature Digest — 2026-10-17 Pulled from PubMed across JSES, JSES International, AJSM, JAAOS, Arthroscopy, JBJS Am, and Bone & Joint Journal. This digest covers 2026-10-10 to 2026-10-17. A quieter week than last: 8 shoulder-specific clinical and translational articles qualified — JSES (4), Arthroscopy (3), and JBJS Am (1). The 7-day yield met the threshold of 8, so the window was not widened; the preceding week (2026-10-02 to 2026-10-10) was already covered in full by last week's digest, which was re-swept through 2026-10-12. The headline is a pair of papers that complete a story begun last week. Seven days ago we covered the 2025 International Consensus Meeting definition of shoulder periprosthetic joint infection, which replaced opinion-based weighting of the minor criteria with statistically derived weights. This week JSES publishes the ASES Revision Arthroplasty / PJI Multicenter Group model that produced those weights: 861 consecutive revision shoulder arthroplasties, with sinus tract or purulence as the outcome, distilled into a seven-variable nomogram with an apparent concordance statistic of 0.90. Alongside it, JBJS Am publishes a Level I randomized noninferiority trial from Rabin Medical Center showing that a surgeon-performed, landmark-guided "shoulder field anesthesia" was noninferior to interscalene block for 48-hour pain after arthroscopic shoulder surgery, with no Horner syndrome or respiratory events and a shorter hospital stay. In the rotator cuff, a Hamburg group reports a prospective comparative cohort of preoperative subacromial autologous conditioned plasma injections, which modestly lowered histologic Bonar and degeneration scores in the supraspinatus at the time of repair, though below the predefined clinically important difference; and the Osaka superior capsule reconstruction group tracks graft angiogenesis with power Doppler ultrasound through the first year, finding vascularity in every fascia lata graft that peaks at about 6 months and then recedes, uncorrelated with pain. In instability, a 149,024-patient PearlDiver study finds nearly 8% of Bankart repair patients visit an emergency department within 90 days, with smoking, Medicaid, and depression the strongest predictors and open repair carrying higher odds than arthroscopic; and a Mayo Clinic Arizona imaging study shows that a congruent-arc distal tibial allograft harvested from the posterior tibia recreates glenoid concavity, whereas the traditional lateral graft actually flattens it. Rounding out the week are a Rothman bibliometric analysis of 506 reverse arthroplasty studies published in JSES over two decades, and a Sun Yat-sen series of customized 3D-printed shoulder arthrodesis prostheses after proximal humerus tumor resection. JSES International, AJSM, JAAOS, and Bone & Joint Journal published no new qualifying shoulder articles in this window. item.title: Shoulder Literature — 2026-10-10
item.itunes:author: Eric R. Wagner, MD, MSc
item.description: Weekly Shoulder Surgery Literature Digest — 2026-10-10 Pulled from PubMed across JSES, JSES International, AJSM, JAAOS, Arthroscopy, JBJS Am, and Bone & Joint Journal. This digest covers 2026-10-02 to 2026-10-10. A much fuller week after two quiet ones: 18 shoulder-specific clinical and translational articles qualified — JSES (10), JSES International (2), Arthroscopy (4), and JBJS Am (2). The 7-day yield cleared the threshold of 8, so the window was not widened. The headline paper is the 2025 International Consensus Meeting definition of shoulder periprosthetic joint infection, led by the Rothman Institute: organism virulence is gone, purulence and a sinus tract remain the only "definite" criteria, and the minor criteria are now statistically weighted from the ASES multicenter PJI dataset into a points-based likelihood scale. Infection runs right through this week — an ASES survey shows nearly 9 in 10 shoulder surgeons still recommend dental antibiotic prophylaxis after TSA, an Osaka series links a low Geriatric Nutritional Risk Index to a roughly sevenfold higher odds of PJI after reverse arthroplasty, and a Duke series of convertible-stem revisions finds unexpected positive cultures in about 1 in 7 "unlikely-PJI" cases, yet only 3% reoperated for infection. In arthroplasty, a 791-shoulder Florida Orthopaedic Institute cohort sets long-term benchmarks for anatomic TSA: 96% survivorship at 10 years, 94% at 15, and anchor-based 10-year PASS, MCID, and SCB thresholds for the ASES score. In the cuff, an Arthroscopy meta-analysis of 9 RCTs finds biologic graft augmentation cuts retear risk by roughly two-thirds; a Yeosu Baek Hospital propensity-matched study finds pseudoparesis does not worsen outcomes after anterior latissimus–teres major transfer; and there are machine-learning, AI-imaging, early-rehabilitation, and PROMIS-adoption papers. Instability brings a 10-year military remplissage series, a 41-patient distal clavicle autograft bone-block series, a Turkish study showing remplissage external-rotation loss doesn't cost patients clinically meaningful outcomes, an adolescent Latarjet systematic review, and a 3D statistical-shape study placing the coracoid more superior in anterior instability. AJSM, JAAOS, and Bone & Joint Journal published no new qualifying shoulder articles in this window. Letters, errata, author replies, editorials, editorial commentaries, and invited commentaries were excluded, as were elbow-only items (a JSES PRP-for-lateral-epicondylitis trial, an elbow arthrodesis review, a distal UCL cadaveric study, a radial head arthroplasty population study, an Essex-Lopresti systematic review, an elbow-RCT loss-to-follow-up review, and a JSES International elbow-ligament graft anatomy study), plus hip, knee, foot/ankle, spine, tumor, and wrist items. item.title: Shoulder Literature — 2026-10-03
item.itunes:author: Eric R. Wagner, MD, MSc
item.description: Weekly Shoulder Surgery Literature Digest — 2026-10-03 Pulled from PubMed across JSES, JSES International, AJSM, JAAOS, Arthroscopy, JBJS Am, and Bone & Joint Journal. This digest covers 2026-09-26 to 2026-10-03. Another short week: 6 shoulder-specific clinical and translational articles qualified — JSES (3), AJSM (1), Arthroscopy (1), and JBJS Am (1). Because the 7-day yield fell below 8, the window was widened to 14 days per protocol; the widening added zero further shoulder papers, since the extra week had already been swept by the 2026-09-26 digest and everything else in it was hip, knee, or commentary. JSES International and Bone & Joint Journal posted no new records of any kind in this window, which accounts for much of the quiet. What did arrive is a well-balanced small set: a rotator cuff salvage series, a biceps tenodesis tension study, a cuff outcomes-prediction paper, a 3D instability-morphology study, a Medicare utilization analysis, and a basic-science tendinopathy model. The most practically useful paper of the week is a Sun Yat-sen comparative cohort asking whether it matters how much tension you set on a long head of the biceps tenodesis. Fifty patients tenodesed in situ at native ("iso") tension were compared with 73 tenodesed after proximal transection at reduced tension. Shear-wave elastography confirmed the techniques really did produce different tendon stiffness, and the isotension group finished with better ASES, Constant, and LHB scores and better elbow-flexion strength, with no difference in pain or Popeye deformity. It is retrospective, and the ASES difference sits near the margin of clinical importance, but it is a rare tenodesis study that measures the variable it claims to be testing. The most clinically reassuring paper is a Yeosu Baek Hospital series showing that middle trapezius tendon transfer for an irreparable supraspinatus tear works as well after a failed cuff repair as it does as a primary operation — 53 patients, MCID achievement above 92% in both groups, and intact transfers on MRI in more than 90%. Elsewhere: a University of Maryland registry study finds that preoperative depression and comorbidity burden predict two-year PROMIS Pain Interference after arthroscopic cuff repair, while better baseline ASES predicts less pain; a West China 3D-CT study finds that a taller-narrower glenoid (higher glenoid index) and a shallower glenoid are present even in the uninjured contralateral shoulder of patients with recurrent anterior instability; a Case Western–University Hospitals Medicare analysis documents a 28% fall in subacromial decompression, a 36% fall in distal clavicle excision, and a 130% rise in biceps tenodesis from 2013 to 2023, with inflation-adjusted reimbursement down roughly a quarter to a third for all three; and an HSS murine impingement model shows CCR2 knockout blunts the early macrophage surge of rotator cuff tendinopathy without improving tendon mechanics. item.title: Shoulder Literature — 2026-09-26
item.itunes:author: Eric R. Wagner, MD, MSc
item.description: Weekly Shoulder Surgery Literature Digest — 2026-09-26 Pulled from PubMed across JSES, JSES International, AJSM, JAAOS, Arthroscopy, JBJS Am, and Bone & Joint Journal. This digest covers 2026-09-19 to 2026-09-26. It is a deliberately short one: only 7 shoulder-specific clinical and translational articles qualified — JSES International (4), Arthroscopy (2), and JBJS Am (1). The reason is straightforward and worth stating up front: the 2026-09-22 digest ran only four days ago and swept an unusually heavy 24-article window, so most of what the seven journals posted this week had already been covered. Per protocol the window was widened to 14 days when the 7-day yield fell below 8, and the widening added zero further shoulder papers — every 14-day extra was either already covered on 2026-09-22 or was a knee/hip/foot item or an editorial commentary. This is a genuinely quiet week, not a missed sweep. What did arrive is heavily weighted toward reconstruction of the difficult shoulder — the malunited proximal humerus, the malunited scapula, the failed posterior stabilization — plus two technology papers on navigation and kinematics and two biomechanics papers. The most clinically sobering paper of the week is a Walter Reed natural-history series on traumatic posterior glenohumeral dislocation in young, high-demand patients. Thirty-three shoulders in a predominantly active-duty military cohort were followed after a confirmed posterior dislocation or subluxation event, and the failure rates are grim in both arms: 61% failed nonoperative management (usually by recurrent dislocation) and 53% failed after surgery, most often requiring revision. Nearly half the operative cohort ended up on permanent duty restriction or never returned to their occupation. Posterior instability in this population is not the benign counterpart of anterior instability, and these numbers belong in the preoperative conversation. The most immediately useful technical paper is a Groningen–Adelaide cadaveric feasibility study of 3D patient-specific cutting and reduction guides for corrective osteotomy of malunited proximal humerus fractures, including a novel humeral-head–tuberosity separation technique for severe malunions with disrupted anatomy. Seven planned osteotomies landed within a median 5.2° of planned rotation and 3.4° of planned valgus — under 10° deviation across the board. This is a feasibility study on Thiel-embalmed specimens, not a clinical series, but it puts a technically forbidding operation on a planned footing. The largest dataset of the week is a navigation study out of NYU using 19,054 navigated total shoulder arthroplasties across 871 surgeons on the Advita GPS platform, asking how faithfully the preoperative plan is actually executed in augmented glenoids. item.title: Shoulder Literature — 2026-09-22
item.itunes:author: Eric R. Wagner, MD, MSc
item.description: Weekly Shoulder Surgery Literature Digest — 2026-09-22 Pulled from PubMed across JSES, JSES International, AJSM, JAAOS, Arthroscopy, JBJS Am, and Bone & Joint Journal. This digest covers 2026-09-12 to 2026-09-22. The window was set to close the gap since the 2026-09-13 digest, and it is a heavy one: 24 shoulder-specific clinical and translational articles qualified — Arthroscopy (8), JSES International (7), JSES (6), JBJS Am (2), and AJSM (1). The single most practice-changing paper is a Level I randomized controlled trial from Geneva and Lausanne. Eighty-six patients undergoing an open Latarjet were randomized to immediate self-rehabilitation with or without three weeks of sling immobilization. At six months the two groups were indistinguishable on every outcome, including graft union and osteolysis — but at two years the no-sling group was 12.5 Rowe points and 7.9 SANE-instability points ahead, was half again as likely to reach a patient acceptable symptom state, and the only two recurrent dislocations in the trial happened in the sling group. The routine post-Latarjet sling now has to justify itself. Running a close second in practical consequence is a Kaiser Permanente registry analysis in the same journal. Across 13,901 primary shoulder arthroplasties, anatomic TSA performed with an Exactech Equinoxe device carried a 1.87-fold adjusted revision hazard versus other devices — a signal that persisted (HR 1.91) when restricted to the implants packaged in the non-conforming bags that triggered the 2024 recall. Notably, no such difference appeared in elective reverse TSA. Anyone carrying an Equinoxe anatomic in their practice population now has a number to counsel with. The rotator cuff dominates the rest of the week. The Duke-led international consensus effort — 97 surgeons from 15 countries — lands in three simultaneous Arthroscopy papers covering diagnosis and posterosuperior repair (Part I), subscapularis, augmentation and tendon transfer (Part II), and reverse arthroplasty, revision and rehabilitation (Part III). The most instructive results are the failures to agree: graft augmentation and superior capsular reconstruction produced 16 statements with no consensus at all in Part II, and Part III found no agreement on any surveillance protocol. On the technical side, a Sydney prospective cohort of 1,000 consecutive undersurface knotless repairs of partial-thickness tears reports a 1.4% retear rate with a visible learning curve flattening after roughly 200 cases; a Seoul deep-learning volumetric study shows that supraspinatus muscle volume recovery at one year tracks tendon healing and independently predicts lower retear odds (OR 0.49 per 10% volume gain); and a Strasbourg series finds that low pain at one month after cuff repair — predicted by an intact subscapularis, no preoperative analgesics, and lower baseline pain — marks a patient whose whole first year runs better by more than the MCID. item.itunes:author: Eric R. Wagner, MD, MSc
item.description: Weekly Shoulder Surgery Literature Digest — 2026-09-13 Pulled from PubMed across JSES, JSES International, AJSM, JAAOS, Arthroscopy, JBJS Am, and Bone & Joint Journal. This digest covers 2026-09-06 to 2026-09-13. It is a light week: 8 shoulder-specific clinical and translational articles qualified, split evenly between JSES (4) and Arthroscopy (4). Because the 7-day haul sat at the sparse threshold, the sweep was widened to 14 days (back to 2026-08-28); every shoulder article in the extra week had already been covered in the 2026-09-07 digest, so the widening added nothing new and is not double-counted here. The week's sharpest clinical message comes from Tampa. In a propensity-matched comparison of lateralized reverse shoulder arthroplasty with versus without a concomitant latissimus dorsi transfer, the transfer bought no additional external rotation and no better ASES improvement — but 96% of the transfer shoulders showed early proximal humeral osseous erosion against 4% of the reverse-alone shoulders. In the rotator cuff, a meta-analysis of five RCTs finds that leukocyte-poor PRP injected at the time of repair nearly halves the structural failure rate (15.9% vs 29.0%) yet moves no patient-reported outcome past its MCID; a Sydney study links shear-wave elastography stiffness to collagen disorganization and mixed cellularity on histology of the torn supraspinatus edge; and a 140,886-patient claims analysis ties alcohol use disorder to a roughly sixfold higher odds of 90-day adverse events after cuff repair, with pneumonia leading the list. Rounding out the week: a Seattle cohort finds that patient-reported allergies do not predict a poor anatomic TSA outcome on their own, but two or more allergies — and specifically allergies to medications other than antibiotics or analgesics — do; an HSS systematic review shows how inconsistently MCID, SCB, and PASS are derived and applied across 39 TSA studies; a Creighton biomechanics study shows a reinforced polyester patch sandwiched in a thin fascia lata graft brings SCR graft strength up to that of a thick graft; and a systematic review of 65 studies of shoulder surgery in contact and collision athletes finds return-to-play reporting too thin to compare across studies. JSES International, AJSM, JAAOS, JBJS Am, and Bone & Joint Journal published no new qualifying shoulder articles in this window. Letters, errata, author replies, editorials, and editorial commentaries were excluded, as were elbow-only, hand/wrist, hip, knee, foot/ankle, spine, and education/practice-management items. Search note: the window was swept by entry date (edat) and create date (crdt) across all seven journals with no keyword filter, and unioned; every record was screened by title and PMIDs were diffed against the 171 already covered in prior digests. item.title: Shoulder Literature — 2026-09-07
item.itunes:author: Eric R. Wagner, MD, MSc
item.description: Weekly Shoulder Surgery Literature Digest — 2026-09-07 Pulled from PubMed across JSES, JSES International, AJSM, JAAOS, Arthroscopy, JBJS Am, and Bone & Joint Journal. This digest covers a 10-day window (2026-08-29 to 2026-09-07) rather than the usual 7 days, because the scheduled Saturday 2026-09-05 run did not execute — the window was extended back to the day after the last digest so that no article fell through the gap. 18 shoulder-specific clinical and translational articles qualified, the largest haul in several weeks, and unusually Arthroscopy (8) outproduced JSES (6). The week's center of gravity is the rotator cuff, and specifically the question of what actually drives healing. A rat model from Xi'an defines a repair-tension "sweet zone" of 0.10–0.12 N/mm² with a bell-shaped relationship between tension and enthesis quality — the first quantitative answer to a question every surgeon settles by feel. A Chinese cohort shows early (<3 weeks) repair of traumatic massive tears beats delayed repair by 6.3 ASES points independent of confounders, while the retear rate stays stubbornly the same. A 5-year MRI series from Korea finds that superior capsular reconstruction grafts thin progressively even when they look intact, and that MR arthrography uncovers retear in 80% of symptomatic patients whom conventional MRI called healed. A systematic review out of Rush then decouples the outcome from the radiograph entirely: PROMs and forward flexion improve after cuff repair, SCR, and tendon transfer regardless of whether the acromiohumeral interval increases at all. On the arthroplasty side, two negative diagnostic papers land in the same issue and point the same direction: arthroscopic pre-revision tissue biopsy had 27–30% sensitivity for periprosthetic joint infection, and three patients with entirely negative biopsies grew ≥2 unexpected positive cultures at revision — a direct sequel to last week's 16S rRNA PCR paper from the same Wisconsin group. A meta-analysis of 2,639 patients finds single-shot interscalene block matches continuous catheters on 24-hour pain with a fourfold lower complication rate and a fraction of the cost. A Medicare analysis of 533,569 shoulder arthroplasties documents a 3.2-fold volume increase with surgeons still 88.9% urban and revision arthroplasty performed essentially nowhere but cities. And a 476,620-procedure UK linked-data study puts shoulder arthroplasty VTE at 1.0% — the lowest of the three major joints — with a 9% decline after the 2018 NICE guidance that hip and knee did not show.
